Hacknet is a great gem of a game. Its primary function is to be a portable 'hacker simulator' and to that extent, it does that quite well. A genre naturally suited for the typing and point-clicking games, hacking inside hacknet, is devoid of large explosions or the rejoice of having brought the world to its knees. It seeks to measure achievement in a world, where humans speak through machines and asking the right question open doors. 

The games' mechanics work on using time and resource allocation, as well relying on the curiosity of the player; who with his magical key, is capable of accessing anyone's cyberspace and playing god, to that extent. Despite this rather dramatic description, the game is mostly that, drama, as it exists between people, mediated through technology. The player is the central arbitrator. Good Story line, would be nice if it was extended, as the gamut of technology topics covered is not really as broad as could be. 

In sum: not a bad way to spend a weekend at home.

This was an incredible game, and I highly recommend it to everyone, especially if you're familiar with or want to learn the UNIX command line (bash).

Hacknet is very well-paced, slowing down and allowing you to "explore" at times while keeping a sense of urgency throughout. At times there will be a ticking clock on screen depending on what you're hacking into, but this is my first gripe with the game: the seconds are never consistent from machine to machine. Sometimes it's 3 seconds per on-screen second, sometimes it's a millisecond per on-screen second. I wish there had been a little more consistency here, because it does take time to figure out exactly how long you have before something bad happens.

Other than the timers, this game really was well-thought-out. And after one playthrough, you can go back and do it again, because [spoiler] many things are procedurally generated, meaning they change with each individual game [/spoiler] . It's also a great puzzle game. I was initially frustrated by how vague some of the instructions were, but I quickly realized that's by design. You're given an endgoal, but you have to figure out exactly what steps to take to make it there. It also helps that many of your missions can be picked from a list, allowing you to either take an easy or hard case, depending on how you feel, without affecting the story.

I really can't recommend this game enough, and I can't wait for the DLC that's about to come out!
10/10 One of the best games I have ever played;  an amazing story running through it and nice little easter eggs/hidden gems which really make it a joy to play.

A very introspective look at UNIX commands and the general actions of hacking - which is basically accurate, but taking out the time required to accomplish these things (for example, you can solve port protocols within a few seconds, but IRL this might take hours).

Basically, if you want the "reality" where you are the hacker in one of these movies (you're not playing the hacker, but ARE the hacker), then this is pretty spot-on. It just removes most of the tedium of the acitivites. This is not to say that the game isn't repetitive; it is, and remains true to its roots as a simulator. By nature, most simulators run off of repetitive actions which require muscle memory and timing in order to complete.

In actual fact, this is more of a puzzle-solving game. However, combined with some funny easter eggs (IRC chats can get hilarious) and honest-to-god methodology on the principles of hacking, this actually becomes enjoyable unless you just want to shoot things in the face (in which case, this is NOT the game for you).

Anyone who wants to work in software QA should be able to play this game comfortably, figure out most of the puzzles, and genuinely enjoy the experience. If you can't, don't take QA as a career. Because this in almost any form is what you do - all day, every day. I know this from 14 years of experience at that job in everything from game development to SAS or security software.

There are a few points I wish there were more of, or more developed. As game, it's pretty linear. There are nice little things like finding additional information on a server which gives you another terminal to hack, or a phone to break into, but these are too few and far between. It could be far more sandboxy if there were a freeform mode for points, which had sets of systems and connected devices which would allow you to randonly investigate things you found on another system. In this, you'd need a points system or something to gain (money, cred, whatever) - which would be a welcome addition to the game. I think another fun mode would be to actually use the system specs for the computer it was running on for memory, etc. as well as randonly generating in-game groups to become involved with, do missions for (from forums, etc.)

I recommend this game, just due to the simulation nature being captured very well. That being said, this game won't be for everyone. Much of the game is tedium and random investigation - which is exactly what hacking is about. One of the best missions which represents this is the "Project Junebug" mission. You're basically let loose to figure out how to accomlish the task, you have a lot of reading to do to catch up on how to accomplish it, and there isn't any handholding. YOU have to do the tasks, to the best of your understanding, and figure out indeed, what those tasks are, and it involves multiple servers, and different methods of having the same outcome.

Let's face it guys and girls: Most of us will never hack the headquarter of a huge and powerful concern. Most of us are actually screwed when we forget the PIN for our smartphone. And thats ok. Nothing to feel bad for.
But still....those classic hacker movies. And this Mr. Robot show. That looks so awesome. But are we interested in dedicating our freetime for our new and perhaps fleeting passion? Learn to program and hack and learn code and whatever. Books! Math! Boring stuff!
Thank God there is Hacknet, a hacking sim reminiscent of the classic game Uplink. And in a good way!

Basically, you are a hacker and you follow a storyline and/or your own ideas and hack your way through files, computer systems, security and whatnot. And, like in real life, the protagonist (you!) sits in front of the computer and does all this incredible hacking stuff from his or her chair. And in a game like this, its about the small things it does: You can click on a computer to connect with it. Or you use command codes and an IP adress. You can look through files with clicking on a button. Or you use, you guessed it, command codes to look through it. The latter feels more authentic, and sometimes, thats what you want. Actually, in my humble opinion, this game is best when you try to use as many written commands as possible. It gives you the feeling to be a real hacker. 

In many games, hacking is an afterthought. A minigame at best. Like in Deus Ex: Hacking belongs to Cyberpunk like awesome armblades, but it is basically connect-the-dots with a nicer color palette. And thats totally cool, cause you dont want to obstruct the core gameplay.
But if you want to feel like a real hacker, disrupting the system chilling in a comfy chair, then look no further than Hacknet. Choose your nickname, learn a few basic commands that the game teaches you and discover your inner anarchist. The game gets more complicated along the way and you have to think a bit more, but thats what you want. Hacking the computer of a smalltown retirement home is one thing, but getting these corporations: Thats the holy grail of cyberpunk-esque hacking, isnt it?

I'm not sure if I want to recommend this game or not. To be honest, I wouldn't really recommend it; but, at the same time, it doesn't really deserve a thumbs down.

The problem is that the game isn't challenging, just tedious. It doesn't take any mental flexibility to complete any of it its challenges, just the ability to follow a routine, patience, and a little bit of attention. but then again, doesn't that make it a pretty accurate simulator of actual hacking?

This gave me a vibe that I thought was unique to Papers, Please: you're following a pretty boring routine, but you're doing it for some sort of purpose, so you keep doing it.

I can't really hit that thumbs down button because it's clear that a lot of work and love was put into this game, and the developer tried hard to get an immersive atmosphere of an actual computer terminal. But even then, the immersion is broken sometimes, such as the in-game imageboard not actually reacting in any way to the things you do to it.

tl;dr I wouldn't recommend this game, but I'm glad it exists, so it gets a thumbs up.
